lines.speaker: A
lines.text: You just watched The Matrix and you want something that feels similar. Not the same genre tag, the same feeling. How would a computer find that?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I'd guess it compares keywords. Is that it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's one way, and the project tries it too. But the main idea is different. SimilityVectorEmbedding is a set of Jupyter notebooks from AlgoÉTS that turn a movie catalog into embeddings, which are lists of numbers where similar films end up close together.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: How do you get a film down to numbers?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: First it builds one piece of text per film: the title, year, genres, actors, director, summary, country, language and writers. In the saved run there are 631 films. A small model called MiniLM reads that text and produces a vector of 384 numbers.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And then they sit in a database?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes, in PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension. When you type a title, even loosely, it finds the closest real title by comparing three-letter chunks. Then it ranks every other film by cosine similarity, which is basically how much two vectors point the same way.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What do you get for The Matrix?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The two sequels come out on top, at about 75 and 73 percent. Then The Mummy, Speed and Con Air show up in the mid-fifties. Nine films pass the fifty percent cut-off.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Can you search with more than one movie?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: You can. Give it several titles and it averages their vectors, so a trilogy pulls the search toward what the three share. You can also rate the titles, and the ratings weight the mix. With The Matrix and Toy Story 2 rated high and The Lion King rated one, the query is mostly the first two.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Is it all PostgreSQL, or does it explore other tools?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It compares several. The same idea runs on Qdrant, there's a keyword version with BM25, and a Neo4j graph that links films through shared genres and people. There's also a local language model you can ask questions in plain words, and a Gradio page showing posters and scores.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So it's a tour of how similarity search can work.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. The companion article tells it as a story, with the original demo animations.
